Migrants sent 700 billion dollars home in remittances in 2024, more than every government's foreign aid combined, and it lands right where it is needed. Mackenzie calls it the most efficient development tool we have.

In Japan he found a government quietly recruiting foreign workers while moving right on immigration in public. The official term for immigrants translates to foreign human resources. He reads it as a preview of debates the US has not had yet.

Mackenzie followed Deepak, a man in western Nepal who commutes seasonally to Delhi, a path his father walked for 20 years before him. The open Nepal-India border lets him go home. Close a border and you don't stop people from leaving. You stop them from coming back.

I just published my conversation with photojournalist Mackenzie Knowles-Coursin, who reports on migration across the global south from his base in Nairobi. It pulled me out of the US enforcement frame in the best way.

Reporting by Perla Trevizo for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune. Read the full investigation:

www.propublica.org/article/camp...

On Monday, his three children sued the companies that ran the facility, alleging guards killed him and citing missed medication doses and improper use of force. DHS initially said he had experienced medical distress.

Dr. Sanjay Basu, a UCSF epidemiologist who reviewed the records, said the pattern in his chart is "the predictable result of erratic psychotropic medication administration in a patient with serious mental illness." His conclusion from the records was systemic neglect.

Staff discussed transferring him to a facility with a higher level of care as early as Oct. 8. The transfer never happened. He was repeatedly placed in segregation cells, which federal standards say should generally be avoided for detainees with serious mental illness.

In early October, guards found him in his cell with a bedsheet around his neck, tied to the door handle. Staff notes dismissed it as a "suicidal gesture" meant to force his release from isolation and concluded hospitalization was "not clinically indicated at this time."

The records show a man in crisis. He banged his head against a wall after he could not afford the charges to call his children in New York, leaving him with a black eye. Staff noted they told him to stop because "he must take care of his brain and his eyes."

Geraldo Lunas Campos had a history of serious mental illness. A nearly 300-page medical examiner's investigative report, reviewed by ProPublica and The Texas Tribune, documents his interactions with medical staff over the months before his death.

A Cuban man held at Camp East Montana complained at least eight times about skipped doses of his antipsychotic medication. He died after an altercation with guards over that medication. A coroner ruled it a homicide. 🧵
